paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when different users can value the same outcomes differently. The environment has several predefined reward components, and a preference vector determines how they combine into a single reward. The agent must learn unknown transitions while accommodating preferences that may be chosen adversarially, rather than following a predictable pattern.

In the online setting, a new preference arrives each episode before the agent chooses how to act. The authors give a model-based algorithm with a nearly minimax optimal regret bound. Regret measures the accumulated cost of learning instead of already knowing how to act well. The bound explicitly accounts for the number of objectives, states, actions, and episode length.

The second setting separates exploration from preferences: the agent first collects experience without a specified preference, then supports arbitrary preferences within a chosen error tolerance. Its trajectory requirement is also nearly optimal. Together, these results quantify how much learning is needed to serve changing objectives, with dependence on the smaller of the objective count and state count.
neurips-2021-accommodating-picky-custome.tldr: The paper gives nearly optimal learning guarantees for agents that must accommodate changing or initially unknown preferences over multiple objectives.

paragraphs: Adversarial training commonly spends substantial computation repeatedly searching for image perturbations that fool a model. This paper proposes a non-iterative training method motivated by where robust models appear to look. Its starting observation is that attribution maps, which indicate image regions associated with a prediction, align more closely with the actual object in robust models than in naturally trained models.

The method enforces object-focused ideas during training. One concerns aligning attribution with the object; another restricts the pixels available for decision-changing perturbations to the object itself. That restriction makes the attack space smaller and therefore weakens the permitted attack. It is a substantive part of the approach, rather than an equivalent formulation of unrestricted image perturbation.

The authors report experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet against several strong attacks. They report gains over existing adversarial-training models with 10–20% extra effort and better adversarial and natural accuracy than the compared methods. The findings support object-focused training as a route to robustness, with the stated perturbation restriction central to understanding the approach.
neurips-2021-adversarial-robustness-with.tldr: A non-iterative, object-focused training approach reports improved clean and adversarial accuracy while restricting perturbations to object pixels.

paragraphs: A variational auto-encoder uses a shared encoder to infer a distribution over hidden representations for each observation. Sharing this encoder makes inference scalable, but does not ensure that two versions of the same meaningful content receive consistent representations. The paper identifies disagreement under meaning-preserving transformations as a problem for representation quality and generalization.

The proposed regularizer compares the encoder's distribution for an observation with its distribution for a randomly transformed version. Training minimizes their Kullback–Leibler divergence, encouraging agreement at the distribution level. The key requirement is that the transformation preserve semantics: the regularizer is intended to suppress sensitivity to changes that should not alter what the observation means.

The authors describe the regularizer as applicable to any VAE and test it on four variants. Representation quality improves throughout their experiments, alongside better generalization. Applied to NVAE, it achieves reported state-of-the-art results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CELEBA. Experiments on 3D data also show better downstream classification, and additional comparisons show that the method can outperform triplet-loss representation learning.
neurips-2021-consistency-regularization-.tldr: Encouraging a VAE to encode meaning-preserving transformations consistently improves representations and generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating several people's 3D poses from multiple cameras often involves costly spatial volumes or assembling separately detected 2D poses. Multi-view Pose transformer, or MvP, instead predicts the 3D joint positions directly from the images. This removes intermediate estimation tasks from the pose pipeline and makes cross-view reasoning part of the prediction model itself.

MvP represents skeleton joints with learned query embeddings that progressively gather information from the different views. A hierarchical representation organizes queries for multiple people, while input-dependent adaptation adjusts them to the images. Projective attention uses geometry to guide which cross-view information each joint combines. A further operation, RayConv, incorporates camera geometry into the image features supporting that attention.

The authors report higher accuracy and substantially greater efficiency than previous state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks. On Panoptic, MvP reaches 92.3% AP25. They also describe an extension to human meshes represented by SMPL, connecting the same general approach to body-shape recovery. The contribution combines a direct prediction pipeline with explicit geometric guidance rather than leaving view fusion entirely unconstrained.
neurips-2021-direct-multi-view-multi-per.tldr: MvP directly predicts multiple people's 3D joints from camera views using learned queries and geometrically guided attention.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generative model involves both the quality of its outputs and the diversity of what it produces. Divergence frontiers provide a framework for representing that trade-off. This paper studies how reliably those frontiers can be estimated from samples, making the evaluation procedure itself an object of statistical analysis.

The authors establish non-asymptotic sample-complexity bounds. These concern finite amounts of data, rather than only describing what happens as the sample size grows without limit. They also introduce frontier integrals, summary statistics that condense information from a frontier. This connects a trade-off representation with quantities that can be used to summarize model performance.

A central estimation issue is missing mass: probability associated with outcomes that do not appear in the observed sample. The paper shows how smoothing methods, including Good–Turing and Krichevsky–Trofimov estimators, can address this problem and achieve faster convergence. Numerical examples from language and vision illustrate the theory. The contribution helps explain both the data requirements of frontier-based evaluation and how estimator choice affects its reliability.
neurips-2021-divergence-frontiers-for-ge.tldr: The paper establishes finite-sample guarantees and improved estimators for evaluating generative models through quality–diversity frontiers.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether resistance to adversarial image perturbations must come from training network weights. The authors report finding subnetworks inside randomly initialized networks whose robust accuracy matches or exceeds that of adversarially trained networks of comparable size. They call these selected subnetworks Robust Scratch Tickets, or RSTs.

Neither the original dense network nor the identified subnetwork requires weight training in this approach. The distinction is between finding a suitable subnetwork and adjusting its weights: the result concerns robustness already available within the random initialization. The authors investigate this phenomenon across models, datasets, sparsity patterns, and attacks, using the experiments to examine how initialization and overparameterization relate to robustness.

They also find that attacks transfer poorly between RSTs with different sparsity ratios drawn from the same dense network. This motivates Random RST Switch, a defense that randomly alternates among such subnetworks. The findings indicate that adversarial training of weights is not indispensable for obtaining robust models in the studied settings, and extend the question of useful random subnetworks to adversarial robustness.
neurips-2021-drawing-robust-scratch-tick.tldr: Selected subnetworks within randomly initialized networks exhibit strong adversarial robustness without training their weights.

paragraphs: The exponential mechanism in differential privacy can require drawing samples from a distribution that is difficult to sample exactly. Replacing that draw with approximate Markov chain Monte Carlo can change both privacy and accuracy. This paper addresses the practical need to specify a privacy budget before running a sampler and obtain a guarantee for its actual finite execution.

The authors combine tools from ergodic theory and perfect simulation to construct exact sampling algorithms with finite runtime. Their construction introduces an intermediate modified target distribution using artificial atoms. The purpose is to make exact sampling available within a Markov-chain implementation, so the privacy analysis need not rely only on eventual convergence.

They also propose a modification that preserves an epsilon-differential-privacy guarantee while improving runtime at some cost to utility. Comparisons consider situations where the additional delta privacy cost of standard MCMC can be calculated explicitly. The results make runtime part of the privacy design problem: the strength of the privacy guarantee, computational cost, and usefulness of the output must be considered together.
neurips-2021-exact-privacy-guarantees-fo.tldr: Exact finite-runtime samplers provide explicit privacy guarantees for the exponential mechanism while exposing trade-offs with runtime and utility.

paragraphs: A strong game-playing agent need not respond effectively to the particular person it faces. This paper studies agents that learn an unknown human opponent's behavior through repeated play and use that knowledge to improve their own performance. The setting also imposes bounds on the human's expected utility during each repetition of the game.

Those bounds allow the framework to express applications where winning is not the only consideration, including continued player engagement and educational games. The authors formulate linear inequalities describing the conditions an agent's strategy must satisfy to keep the human's expected utility between the specified lower and upper thresholds. These constraints concern expected utility, rather than guaranteeing a particular outcome in every individual play.

The constraint formulation is incorporated into an upper confidence bound algorithm. The authors prove sublinear regret and show that the utility constraints hold with high probability at each iteration. They also evaluate convergence on standard sequential-game testbeds. The result connects learning to exploit an opponent with explicit, probabilistic protection of the intended experience for that opponent.
neurips-2021-exploiting-opponents-under-.tldr: An online game-playing algorithm learns to exploit opponents while respecting bounds on their expected utility with high probability.

paragraphs: Federated learning must often combine devices with very different processing power and network bandwidth. A single model size can exclude weaker devices or constrain everyone to the capacity of the least capable participant. FjORD addresses this system heterogeneity by allowing clients to work with different model widths according to their capabilities.

Its central mechanism, Ordered Dropout, organizes network knowledge into an ordered, nested structure. Smaller submodels can be extracted from that structure without retraining. The authors also show that Ordered Dropout is equivalent to singular value decomposition for linear maps. That equivalence is specific to the linear setting; the broader framework applies the nested-model idea to neural networks.

FjORD combines Ordered Dropout with self-distillation in federated training. The design makes different client model sizes parts of a shared structured model, rather than treating device capacity as a single global limit. Evaluations with convolutional and recurrent networks across multiple modalities report consistent, significant gains over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving the nested structure. These findings support adapting model capacity to participating devices.
neurips-2021-fjord-fair-and-accurate-fed.tldr: FjORD uses nested submodels and self-distillation to adapt federated learning to clients with different computational capabilities.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can connect distant image regions, but standard self-attention has computation that grows quadratically with sequence length. This becomes especially expensive when high-resolution feature maps are needed for dense predictions. The Glance-and-Gaze Transformer addresses that cost while retaining mechanisms for both broad image relationships and nearby visual detail.

The architecture has two parallel branches. The Glance branch applies self-attention within adaptively dilated partitions of the input. This arrangement achieves linear complexity while maintaining a global receptive field, allowing information from widely separated locations to influence the representation. The Gaze branch uses depth-wise convolution to contribute local image context that complements the Glance features.

The human-inspired naming therefore corresponds to a concrete division of computation: attention handles broad relationships through a cheaper partitioned structure, and convolution supplies local context. The authors report consistently better performance than previous state-of-the-art transformers across several vision tasks and benchmarks. The empirical findings support combining these two forms of processing as an efficient way to preserve both global reach and local information.
neurips-2021-glance-and-gaze-vision-tran.tldr: Glance-and-Gaze combines linear-complexity global attention with local convolution to improve efficiency and reported vision-task performance.

paragraphs: Neural networks can have many low-loss solutions, raising the question of which ones gradient-based training selects. One proposed explanation for generalization is a preference for solutions with large classification margins. This paper investigates when training actually reaches a globally optimal margin and how that behavior relates to a preference for simpler classifiers.

The main positive result concerns two-layer networks with Leaky ReLU activations, trained using gradient flow on data that are both linearly separable and symmetric. Under those conditions, the authors establish global margin optimality regardless of network width. This removes the infinite or exponentially large width requirements present in some earlier results, while retaining explicit assumptions on the data and training dynamics.

The analysis also offers theoretical support for an early-training bias toward linear or other simple solutions. However, the paper demonstrates that the favorable margin result is fragile: a simple manipulation of the data can make gradient flow converge to a linear classifier with a suboptimal margin. Simplicity bias can therefore coexist with failure to find the best-margin solution.
neurips-2021-gradient-descent-on-two-lay.tldr: Gradient flow achieves globally optimal margins for two-layer Leaky ReLU networks under specific data assumptions, but small data changes can undermine that result.

paragraphs: In sequential learning, incorrectly labeled examples can remain in the training set long after they arrive. Methods that only inspect suspicious new examples leave earlier mistakes with no further opportunity for correction. CINCER addresses this by asking a human supervisor to resolve conflicts involving both incoming examples and previously collected data.

When a new example appears suspicious, CINCER finds a training example that the model considers strongly incompatible with it. The annotator can then relabel either example or both. The counter-example serves as an explanation of why the model is concerned, making the query a concrete comparison rather than an unexplained request to reconsider a label.

Counter-examples are selected for both incompatibility and influence, so correcting them can provide useful information to the model. CINCER uses an efficient, robust approximation to influence functions based on the Fisher information matrix. The empirical evaluation reports substantially better data and models when counter-examples are also cleaned, especially with this approximation. The approach turns an explanation into an opportunity to repair the model's existing training history.
neurips-2021-interactive-label-cleaning-.tldr: CINCER improves label cleaning by showing humans conflicting example pairs and allowing corrections to both new and past data.

paragraphs: Many time series of interest are totals or aggregates built from finer-grained time series. MixSeq investigates whether forecasting those underlying series can improve estimates of the aggregate. The motivation is that directly modeling the total may leave useful structure in its individual contributors unexamined.

The analysis assumes that the microscopic time series come from an unknown mixture of probability distributions. The authors show theoretically that identifying the true hidden mixture components could reduce the variance of component-level estimates and thereby improve aggregate estimation. The condition matters: the argument links improvement to recovering the underlying components, rather than promising that any grouping of time series will help.

The proposed model, Mixture of Seq2seq, learns to cluster microscopic series through an end-to-end mixture architecture. Each component is a sequence-to-sequence model with its own parameters, allowing different groups to have different temporal behavior. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report superior performance. The approach connects a statistical reason for separating latent groups with a neural sequence-modeling method for learning those groups.
neurips-2021-mixseq-connecting-macroscop.tldr: MixSeq groups fine-grained time series with a mixture of sequence models to improve forecasting of their aggregate.

paragraphs: Visual representations learned mainly from global image features may be less suited to tasks that require precise local predictions. MST addresses this mismatch in self-supervised transformer training. Its objective is to retain broad semantic information while explicitly learning local context and the spatial organization of an image.

The method dynamically masks image-patch tokens using information from multi-head self-attention maps. This selection is designed to preserve crucial structure during self-supervised learning. A global image decoder then recovers masked and remaining tokens, maintaining spatial information. Masking and reconstruction thus connect the training signal to local image content while keeping a global view of the image.

The experiments report benefits across classification and dense prediction datasets. With DeiT-S and 300 epochs of pretraining, MST reaches 76.9% top-1 linear-evaluation accuracy, exceeding the stated supervised and DINO comparisons. With 100 epochs of pretraining, it reaches 42.7% mAP on MS COCO detection and 74.04% mIoU on Cityscapes segmentation. These results support the usefulness of its spatially informed pretraining beyond whole-image classification.
neurips-2021-mst-masked-self-supervised-.tldr: MST uses attention-guided masking and image reconstruction to learn representations that retain both global meaning and local spatial detail.

paragraphs: Applying reinforcement learning often requires more than specifying what success looks like. A reward function must also provide a useful learning signal along the way, which can demand substantial manual design. This paper reframes goal-directed learning as inferring policies that produce desired outcomes, making the outcome itself central to the formulation.

The authors develop a variational inference objective for this policy-inference problem. From that objective, they derive a shaped reward function that can be learned through interactions with the environment. They also derive a probabilistic Bellman backup operator, connecting the inference formulation to a rule for updating the quantities used in learning.

These components lead to an off-policy algorithm for goal-directed tasks. In experiments spanning manipulation and locomotion, the method produces effective goal-reaching behavior without hand-crafted reward functions. The reported result shows how an inference-based formulation can supply both the reward signal and the learning update in those tasks. Its practical significance is reducing the need to manually engineer rewards that make a specified goal learnable.
neurips-2021-outcome-driven-reinforcemen.tldr: A variational inference formulation learns reward shaping from interaction and supports effective goal-directed behavior without hand-crafted rewards in the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers knowledge from labeled source data to an unlabeled target distribution. Training usually combines source classification with a domain-alignment objective. The paper points out that their gradients can conflict: improving a weighted sum may still damage one component, limiting the solutions reached by ordinary combined-objective optimization.

ParetoDA controls the overall update direction to encourage cooperative progress across objectives. To guide that progress toward useful target predictions, it introduces a surrogate loss that imitates target classification. A prediction-refinement mechanism uses domain labels through Bayes' theorem to support this surrogate, despite the absence of target class labels.

The method also dynamically adjusts its optimization preference using the surrogate-loss gradient on held-out, unlabeled target data. This supplies guidance when an appropriate weighting scheme is not known beforehand. The theoretical analysis establishes that the held-out data can guide optimization without being overfitted by it. Experiments on image classification and semantic segmentation demonstrate effectiveness. The central contribution is treating adaptation as a problem of coordinating competing update directions, with target-oriented guidance throughout training.
neurips-2021-pareto-domain-adaptation-19.tldr: ParetoDA coordinates conflicting adaptation objectives using gradient control and a target-oriented surrogate derived from unlabeled target data.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning must transfer what a model learned from training categories to different categories at evaluation. This paper examines an image cue that can interfere with that transfer: the background. The authors empirically identify background information as a shortcut that helps classification within training categories but does not generalize beyond those categories in the studied setting.

That finding distinguishes success on familiar categories from learning features useful for new ones. A background cue can make the original classification problem easier while failing to provide transferable knowledge about the foreground object. The paper therefore connects the category gap in few-shot learning to which parts of an image the learner uses.

The proposed framework, COSOC, addresses this problem by extracting foreground objects during both training and evaluation. It does so without additional supervision, making foreground extraction part of the solution rather than requiring extra annotations. Extensive experiments on inductive few-shot tasks demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The results support foreground-focused processing as a way to reduce the influence of the identified background shortcut when transferring to new categories.
neurips-2021-rectifying-the-shortcut-lea.tldr: COSOC extracts foreground objects without extra supervision to counter background shortcuts that hinder few-shot transfer to new categories.

paragraphs: SEAL studies how a robot can adapt perception models trained on internet images without collecting additional human labels. Its approach makes movement part of learning: a pretrained perception model helps train an exploration policy, and the observations gathered during exploration are used to improve perception.

A 3D semantic map links these two processes. It provides an intrinsic reward for learning where to explore, while also supporting automatic labeling through consistency across space and time. Label propagation connects observations using that shared 3D structure. The map therefore serves both as guidance for action and as a source of supervision for what the agent sees.

The authors demonstrate improvements in object detection and instance segmentation by letting the agent move through training environments. They further show that the improved perception model can improve Object Goal Navigation. This closes the action–perception loop: perception supports exploration, exploration supplies training observations, and stronger perception supports subsequent behavior. The self-supervised adaptation builds on existing image-trained models while avoiding extra labels for the robot's gathered observations.
neurips-2021-seal-self-supervised-embodi.tldr: SEAL uses active exploration and 3D consistency to improve robot perception without extra labels, then uses that improvement to aid navigation.

paragraphs: Self-supervised tasks can help a GAN discriminator avoid forgetting, but a separate transformation-prediction task may not align with the generator's goal. This paper attributes that mismatch to self-supervised classifiers that do not account for the generator's distribution. It proposes making transformation learning part of the real-versus-fake discrimination task itself.

The method augments GAN labels with information about data transformations. A single label-augmented discriminator replaces the separate discriminator and self-supervised classifier. It considers both generated and real distributions under each transformation, then supplies their discrepancy as a signal for optimizing the generator. This makes the additional supervision directly relevant to distinguishing generated samples from real data.

The theoretical result shows that the optimal generator could converge to reproduce the real data distribution. That is a statement about the formulation's possible optimum, rather than a guarantee for every training run. Empirically, the method significantly outperforms previous self-supervised and data-augmentation GANs on generative modeling and representation learning benchmarks. The results support integrating the auxiliary task with the adversarial objective.
neurips-2021-self-supervised-gans-with-l.tldr: Augmenting real/fake labels with transformation information aligns GAN self-supervision with generation and improves reported modeling and representation results.

paragraphs: Shape As Points represents 3D shapes using oriented point clouds while providing a differentiable route to a surface mesh. The paper revisits this explicit representation because neural implicit representations, despite their flexibility, can require slow inference and careful initialization. Its goal is to combine lightweight points with the surface structure available from a mesh.

The central component is a differentiable version of Poisson Surface Reconstruction. Given oriented points, a GPU-accelerated solver produces an implicit indicator field that bridges the points and the mesh. Because this bridge is differentiable, surface reconstruction objectives such as Chamfer distance can support end-to-end optimization of the representation.

The authors report that SAP is more interpretable and lightweight than neural implicit representations, with inference accelerated by an order of magnitude. It also produces watertight manifold surfaces without prescribing their topology, a stated advantage over other explicit representations. Demonstrations include reconstruction from unoriented point clouds and learning-based reconstruction. The contribution makes the conversion from an editable point representation to a coherent surface part of the optimization process.
neurips-2021-shape-as-points-a-different.tldr: A differentiable Poisson reconstruction layer connects oriented point clouds to watertight meshes for efficient end-to-end shape reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper studies first-order algorithms for monotone variational inequalities when the information available to the optimizer is noisy. It develops a shared framework encompassing dual averaging, dual extrapolation, and optimistic gradient methods, including adaptive and non-adaptive versions. The focus is how convergence depends on the kind of randomness affecting the problem.

For cocoercive problems, the authors first establish optimal rates when the noise profile is known. Absolute noise yields an error rate of order one over the square root of the iteration count, while relative noise allows a rate of order one over that count. The distinction matters because the achievable speed depends on the structure of the uncertainty.

They then analyze an adaptive method that achieves the corresponding rates without prior knowledge of noise variance or the operator's cocoercivity constant. It adjusts across the two noise cases without being told which rate to target. The analysis also shows that an extra-gradient proxy step is unnecessary for these optimal rates. The universality result thus concerns adaptation within the stated problem and noise conditions.
neurips-2021-sifting-through-the-noise-u.tldr: An adaptive first-order method attains optimal rates for two noise regimes without prior noise parameters or an extra-gradient proxy step.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic L-natural-convex minimization, a problem that extends stochastic submodular minimization. The objective is to find a solution close to optimal despite randomness. The authors develop the first polynomial-time algorithms for this problem that return a near-optimal solution with high probability, providing both computational and probabilistic guarantees.

A new truncation operation further reduces the algorithms' computational complexity. When applied to stochastic submodular functions, the resulting complexity is lower than that of existing algorithms for that setting. The paper also provides a strongly polynomial approximation algorithm. Execution requires no prior knowledge of the objective beyond its L-natural-convex structure, making that structural assumption central to the methods.

Alongside the algorithms, the authors derive a lower bound on the computation needed to achieve a high-probability error guarantee. This supplies a benchmark for understanding the inherent difficulty of reliable approximate optimization. Numerical experiments illustrate the efficiency predicted by the theory. The contribution therefore combines broader problem coverage, reduced computational requirements, and an analysis of what obtaining reliable solutions necessarily costs.
neurips-2021-stochastic-l-natural-convex.tldr: New algorithms efficiently approximate stochastic L-natural-convex minima with high-probability guarantees and improve complexity for stochastic submodular minimization.

paragraphs: In continuous-control reinforcement learning, pessimistic value estimates help counter errors introduced by function approximation. However, pessimism can also discourage exploration. This paper examines that tension and finds that the most effective degree of optimism can differ between tasks and change as learning proceeds within a task.

Tactical Optimistic and Pessimistic estimation, or TOP, makes this choice adaptive. The actor-critic framework switches online between optimistic and pessimistic value learning. It treats the choice as a multi-arm bandit problem, allowing experience to inform which estimation approach to use. This makes the handling of uncertainty part of the learning process rather than a fixed setting chosen in advance.

Across a series of continuous-control tasks, TOP outperforms compared methods with fixed optimism levels. The authors also report a new state of the art in challenging environments with pixel observations. These findings support changing estimation tactics during training rather than assuming one degree of caution is best throughout. The proposed changes are simple to implement, and the authors suggest they could fit many off-policy algorithms.
neurips-2021-tactical-optimism-and-pessi.tldr: TOP learns when to use optimistic or pessimistic value updates, improving on fixed choices in the reported continuous-control experiments.

paragraphs: Motion can reveal coherent objects without requiring their semantic categories to be known. This paper uses that idea to learn segmentation from unlabeled video. Its model separates appearance from movement so that learning how frames relate can also teach it which image regions belong together as objects.

An appearance pathway segments individual RGB images into coherent regions. A motion pathway predicts a flow vector for each region between neighboring frames. Together, the pathways construct a representation called segment flow. Training uses this representation to reconstruct one frame from another, supplying self-supervision without object annotations in the video pretraining corpus.

The pretrained model is evaluated in three distinct uses. It can segment a primary object from a single image in a zero-shot setting, segment moving objects in video with unsupervised test-time adaptation, and support semantic segmentation after supervised fine-tuning on labeled images. The authors report encouraging results across these tasks. The distinction between these uses matters: unlabeled video provides the initial learning signal, while semantic segmentation additionally uses labeled fine-tuning.
neurips-2021-the-emergence-of-objectness.tldr: Separating appearance and motion during video reconstruction teaches object regions that support zero-shot and adapted segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning produces candidate policies and value functions from existing data, but choosing between them is itself difficult. Off-policy evaluation can help estimate policy quality, yet often introduces another learned function with its own hyperparameters. This creates a circular tuning problem: selecting a policy requires selecting or tuning its evaluator.

The paper develops hyperparameter-free policy-selection algorithms based on BVFT, a theoretical approach to choosing value functions. The authors demonstrate effectiveness on discrete-action benchmarks, including Atari. The contribution targets the selection stage, giving a way to compare outputs from different training procedures without simply adding another set of tuning choices to that stage.

Continuous-action domains present an additional difficulty: poor critics can degrade selection performance. To address this, the authors combine BVFT with off-policy evaluation, drawing on the strengths of both approaches. This combination also yields a hyperparameter-tuning method for Q-function-based evaluation with theoretical guarantees. The paper thus offers both a direct selection approach and a hybrid response to the explicitly identified problem of unreliable critics.
neurips-2021-towards-hyperparameter-free.tldr: BVFT-based methods reduce tuning demands in offline policy selection, with an evaluation-based extension addressing poor critics in continuous-action domains.
